SAFFRON

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
At R200,000 rand for 1 kg, Saffron is the most expensive spice. However, SA farmers have tried and failed for years to produce a viable, sellable crop. But that was until now.

Unique Selling Point:
The land of Saffron



In 2016 Northern Cape farm Bennie Englebrecht decided to try planting SAFFRON. Despite previous farmers trying and abandoning the challenge quite quickly in South Africa. Bennie managed to grow excellent crops (based on both smell and flavour). Saffron is the MOST expensive spice in the world at R200,000 for one kilogram. Englebrecht however took several years to make the saffron profitable because the downer about it is that it takes 150,000 crocus sativus flowers to yield ONE kilogram – and that means you need labour – each corm/flower/bulb producers 3 red threads (stigma’s - tiny thin red threat part of the flower) The production is very labour intensive, however the flowers are frost resistant and don’t need much water – but lots of heat – which is perfect for karoo like conditions.

Engelbrecht created “Saffricon” and is the managing director – he has tried and tested his crop over 4 years (his farm is between Williston and calvinia in the northern cape (about 4.5 hours from cape town).

Based on his quality – he had interest from Bahrain who believes there is a strong demand for this product internationally. The only other country that has been successful is Iran – and that’s because the majority of its labour force are woman who are paid $5 per day. But its not just used as a spice. Its also used for medicine, dyes and cigarettes. Englebrecht came up with an idea to assist local farmers to start their own crops – his company company is now making saffron bulbs available for around R450,000 for 150,000 of these so-called corms, which should cover a quarter hectare, as part of growing contracts.




Summary:
He is doing this to solve a two fold problem: 1. To ensure that the market grows and assists developing farmers – this week he is in northern pretoria assisting up and coming potential farmers beginning their crops, ad 2. To find out where else in south Africa it will grow successfully. Within three years, peak production should deliver between 1kg and 5kg saffron a hectare. While the sterile flowers are delicate, they only need 250mm to 300m in irrigation, are frost resistant and can withstand temperatures of minus 15 degrees Celsius.

Engelbrecht believes the plants are best suited to the Karoo, but Saffricon is currently testing in KwaZulu-Natal and elsewhere as well. Plans are in place that could see South Africa becoming a significant player in the farming and export of saffron. For the South African economy, this offers an invaluable source of foreign income from exports, whilst also assisting in establishing emerging, small-scale farmers - Furthermore, it offers commercial farmers an alternative source of income through diversification.




Further information:
ABOUT SAFFRICON:

This will be accomplished through an outgrower (contract grower) system based on three-year contracts with farmers. “We supply the farmers with our saffron corms (bulbs), which they then plant and cultivate before harvesting the saffron threads (made up of the crimson-coloured stigmas and styles) and selling the annual crop back to us. The corms multiply underground, on average, about three times per year – that means if one corm is planted in year one, you will, on average, have three corms in year two, nine in year three, 27 in year four, and so on.
“The corms are sold back to Saffricon after year three, hence farmers’ take-up is guaranteed, and they have a double-income potential: from the annual saffron harvest, as well as from the multiplied corms.”

Saffricon has started marketing the outgrower system to prospective saffron farmers and expect to have built sufficient corm stock by next year to start gaining momentum. “This year, there is limited corm stock available and only a few hand-picked outgrowers will be supplied with the product. But by 2022, we should be able to help many more. So, interested parties should start placing orders with Saffricon (www.saffricon.co.za) as soon as possible in order to not be disappointed.”

One farmer who is trying this: Corne Liebenberg of agriculture company Laeveld Agrochem is trying to grow this in Northern Pretoria.

“LAC wants to assist and uplift as far as possible, and the saffron venture offers many farmers that are currently under pressure an alternative option, whilst at the same time giving small-scale farmers an opportunity with solid prospects.

“It is ideal for niche farming – a huge growth area for the South African economy and something that LAC is very passionate about. The initial capital outlay is manageable, relatively little space is required (250m² can accommodate 15 000 corms), and Saffricon will assist with training to bring new farmers up to speed,” says Liebenberg.

“The outgrower (contract grower) system will uplift especially rural communities and give them a means to not only provide for their basic necessities, but also assist them to establish their own businesses with good growth possibilities. Concomitantly, the farmer does not have to wait very long for his return as is the case with many other crops. The above-ground plant growth and eventual harvesting of the flowers happen relatively quickly after the corm is planted.

The farming of saffron is also ideally suited to the South African climate – which, in the last few years, has gone through a harsh drought – as it requires much less water compared to many of the large traditional crops in South Africa,” adds Liebenberg.
Where South Africa’s most prevalent annual crops require roughly between 500-800mm of irrigation per season, saffron – a winter crop grown from March to October – needs between 250mm and 300mm per season.

Liebenberg continues: “Saffron can be grown in almost any environment, in conditions that are traditionally not ideally suited for most kinds of agriculture – such as the Northern Cape, which actually suits the cultivation of saffron. Hence it allows for the production of profitable vegetation from unprofitable soil.

Furthermore, not only is the saffron plant frost-resistant, but it is also protected from adverse weather elements like hail for a large part of the year because of its corms being underground. The latter, and the fact that the corms are not edible, will hopefully also keep it out of the hands of petty criminals looking for food.”

In South Africa, saffron (sometimes referred to as “red gold”) retails for as much as R250/g (or R250 000/kg). The hefty price tag is attributed to the labour-intensive harvesting methods followed – from picking the flowers to removing the threads – which is all done by hand. According to Engelbrecht, 150 000 flowers are needed for 1kg of saffron. “And there are three threads per flower, which means 450 000 (dried) threads are needed for 1kg of saffron. The return per hectare, in year three when production peaks, can vary between 1kg to 5kg.”

GROWTH;

Engelbrecht foresees solid growth prospects for the international saffron market, primarily because world demand far exceeds supply.
According to a report by Grand View Research, the global saffron market size was valued at US$881.7 million (about R13.4 billion) in 2019, with expected compound annual growth of 7.3%, reaching US$1.6 billion (about R22.4 billion) in 2027. Grand View Research base their findings on a growing food industry, improved standard of living, and increasing consumer disposable income.


THE PLAN:

We can film Englebrecht handing out parcels to small scale farmers in north of pretoria - interview the farmers as well as Englebrecht. See him explaining it etc. He has some video and photos of his property and plants. We would just go with Wimpie for the day and get this.

Then:

Fly into cape town, rent car and go with a camera man to Calvinia (4.5 - 5 hours). Film them planting - next week wednesday - maybe I fly up friday and stay with my parents over weekend and spend some time with them. Then go. After I see them planting and see the farm, then I can go and film nicky's story in Springbok - 2-3 hours away from Calvinia. We spent a day and a half getting nicky's case studies etc they are in and around the area. Then we drive back to cape town. and I fly back from there.

I think that's the most economical way of doing it.

Then for my story - the SAFFRON blooms at end of April - so we could wait until then to see if being picked - i do have visuals of it though. And I am going to do a link by the spice at a market. So we can go to pretoria to get visuals of it blooming or we dont wait for it.... up to you.

ROUGH COST:

Car Rental: X4 days = R2,000

Flight to cape town and return = R2,500

Camera man: 3 days filming, 1 travel day. We can put it down to 1.5 half days to each shoot. So these shoots would likely need 3 days each to be successful.

R18,000 - R20,000 for 4 days at R4,500- R5,000 (I need to find a camera man willing to do it for that price)

Stories both have legs and would need to 10 minutes each to make it worth the trip.

If you want to make saffron 8 minutes then that's fine, but potentially then we need another story in cape town to make it more feasible?



Farm – northern cape –

Explain schedule – packing starter packs not give out new packs for new growers – they are putting 500 forms in a starter pack for people to test it in the area, and next year we can properly roll it out.

In pretoria this week – next week Wednesday starting to plant… planting season starts now. Flowers will come in mid-april-end of April.

flight to cape town +-2,500
car +- 2 day rental and petrol to Williston Northern cape from cape town R3,000
1 night stay X 2 (camera man) = R2,000

Script:



You might not recognize this exotic purple flower, but it’s testing South African farmers who have signed up for the challenge of carefully cultivating it to produce the spice known as SAFFRON!
THIS IS RED GOLD…EACH FRAGRANT STRAND PRECIOUS…AND CAN TRANSFORM ANY DISH… IT IS THE WORLDS MOST EXPENSIVE SPICE AT R200,000 A KILO…SAFFRON WAS FIRST CULTIVATED IN ANCIENT GREECE…TODAY ITS MAINLY GROWN IN IRAN, MOROCCO, INDIA… AND NOW IN SOUTH AFRICA.
Bennie Englebrecht left his television producing gig 8 years ago returning to what he calls his “boer” roots to farm. Although others had tried and failed to grow export quality saffron, Englebrecht refused to be beaten by a flower.
B: Strangely enough my wife said to me, this is going to work. And a lot of people said, you're absolutely crazy. What makes you think that you can grow it if nobody else has done it before?
THE SPICE IS THE STIGMA OF THE CROCUS SATIVAS FLOWER… TO COLLECT ONE KILOGRAM TAKES ABOUT 150,000 OF THESE FLOWERS AS EACH ONE ONLY HAS THREE STIGMAS… THAT’S THE RED THREADS YOU SEE HERE…NOT ONLY IS IT LABOUR INTENSIVE, BUT PAINSTAKING.
Englebrecht and his team spend days picking the stigmas from the flowers – which is a mundane and backbreaking task. The saffron rush happens on this isolated farm in the Northern Cape - between Williston and Calvinia.
B: I call them my children
He believes Saffron has its own fighting personality.
B: It needs you to look after it and you need to feel it and be part of it. I love what I do, I'm very passionate about this
This two acre plot is where his saffron experiment, as well as his patience, has been tried and tested with these corms or bulbs.
Today, we are preparing the land field for this year's saffron, all these corms that are here are from last year's harvest. And so they went dormant, um, and now they starting to wake up. So now it's time to plant them. With saffron you plant 40 days later, you get your fruit and then the rest of the season the bulbs multiply under the ground. And in October it goes into dormancy till about February with wakes up again and starts the process all by itself.
Englebrecht has found that the multiplication underground takes 3 years to reap the most profitable yield, so while he was literally - waiting for flowers to grow - he came up with an “out grower” business strategy – called SAFFRICON which rents out the corms to other farmers creating a new market, but also strategically finding out where else the fussy flower will grow successfully.
Saffricon decided that we we're not selling corms. We're renting them out basically for three years. And then after three years, because they multiply, um, up to twenty seven times in three years, um, we buy all those corms back again from those outgrowers.
Engelbrechts farm-hands joke that they’ve broken their backs with Englebrecht, not for him.
AFRIKAANS – I’m
I want them to grow with me in this business. And to take ownership. and you can see the pride.
This soccer-field sized crop will rake in a million rand. Englebrecht’s team are also hand delivering these starter-packs to small scale farmers around the country.
B: I don't want to give out hectres of this, this, and then everybody is cross with me because it didn't work. And the best thing to do is to make sure that it works with you. And then next year you can make an educated decision by yourself.
SAFFRON PROVIDES A BEAUTIFUL GOLDEN COLOUR AND A PUNGEANT, AROMATIC FLAVOUR TO FOOD… THE RED GOLD THREATS ARE SOLD IN A FEW STRANDS OR IN GROUND FORM. IT ALSO HAS MANY OTHER USES – IN MEDICINE, PERFUME AND DYES… AND IT’S THE COLOUR AND SMELL THAT DETERMINE THE QUALITY.
We met up with the team in Johannesburg who have found an international buyer.
B: Iran is the biggest producer. They do about 300 tons of saffron a year.
Mac: This is a korm? “Komm saam met my hahaha”
B: We just got feedback, from a sheikh in Bahrain that wants to buy all our from that. The quality's extremely good.
M: How much would saffron this much be about?
B: I would say that's about five, five grams, about ten grand.
M: Ten grand. So I'm holding ten grand. Yeah. Yeah. Ten thousand. Yeah. Wow. And to filll this?
B: two day's work depending on how many people you have working with you and doing
M: Two days just for this much?
B: Yeah.
Farm worker
NORTH OF PRETORIA, A SMALL SCALE FARMING PROJECT HAS BEEN SET UP TO PLANT SAFFRON. MARCH IS PLANTING SEASON, AND BY THE END OF APRIL, THE FLOWERS WILL BE READY TO HARVEST.
Jaco Fick is a painter – but upon hearing about the lucrative opportunity decided it was worth digging up his family’s plot and planting the picky flower.
M: When did this operation start?
J: Basically from breaking soil, uh, three weeks, three weeks.
M: Wow. And are you excited?
J: Yes, we are. We are totally excited. We are really looking forward to what this can actually become.
Adlib
J: Basically if we are going to do it we need to do it 100%.
Farming solutions expert Corné Liebenberg shares Englebrecht’s vision, but also SAFFRICON. As co-director, he’s assisting investors in cultivating the spice - successfully.
Mac: What's the excitement around saffron?
Corne: Most probably, the potential income stream. We started I think about 300 of the corms and now there’s more than two million. So it's a good success story. You have to create a market and a good brand and I think that’s going to create a bigger market, because currently the market is way higher than the supply.
Mac: So kids, we can stop saying Old MacDonald had a farm. They can say old Macfarlane had a farm...
Englebrecht has gifted a starter pack to the local Calvinia municipality hoping they become as excited about the flower as he is. Back on the farm it seems even the weather - which has brought rain - is spurring on Englebrecht to succeed.
E: Very, very nice surprise last night when 25. Mm. And, um, basically the soil was prepared for us for today.
Using modern farming techniques like a planting machine, the team cut down a week long process to only a few hours.
For now, it's very crucial that we don't go overboard and go too quickly we need to do our homework and make sure that it works right now.
Engelbrechts ‘can do’ attitude will hopefully see that careful homework rewarded… for now though, he’s content to while away the time waiting for his saffron to grow, reading his own poetry on his stoep in the vast karoo landscape…(poetry)

Carte Blanche HD TEST ACCOUNT 18 August 2021 Script: You might not recognize this exotic purple flower, but it’s testing South African farmers who have signed up for the challenge of carefully cultivating it to produce the spice known as SAFFRON! THIS IS RED GOLD…EACH FRAGRANT STRAND PRECIOUS…AND CAN TRANSFORM ANY DISH… IT IS THE WORLDS MOST EXPENSIVE SPICE AT R200,000 A KILO…SAFFRON WAS FIRST CULTIVATED IN ANCIENT GREECE…TODAY ITS MAINLY GROWN IN IRAN, MOROCCO, INDIA… AND NOW IN SOUTH AFRICA. Bennie Englebrecht left his television producing gig 8 years ago returning to what he calls his “boer” roots to farm. Although others had tried and failed to grow export quality saffron, Englebrecht refused to be beaten by a flower. B: Strangely enough my wife said to me, this is going to work. And a lot of people said, you're absolutely crazy. What makes you think that you can grow it if nobody else has done it before? THE SPICE IS THE STIGMA OF THE CROCUS SATIVAS FLOWER… TO COLLECT ONE KILOGRAM TAKES ABOUT 150,000 OF THESE FLOWERS AS EACH ONE ONLY HAS THREE STIGMAS… THAT’S THE RED THREADS YOU SEE HERE…NOT ONLY IS IT LABOUR INTENSIVE, BUT PAINSTAKING. Englebrecht and his team spend days picking the stigmas from the flowers – which is a mundane and backbreaking task. The saffron rush happens on this isolated farm in the Northern Cape - between Williston and Calvinia. B: I call them my children He believes Saffron has its own fighting personality. B: It needs you to look after it and you need to feel it and be part of it. I love what I do, I'm very passionate about this This two acre plot is where his saffron experiment, as well as his patience, has been tried and tested with these corms or bulbs. Today, we are preparing the land field for this year's saffron, all these corms that are here are from last year's harvest. And so they went dormant, um, and now they starting to wake up. So now it's time to plant them. With saffron you plant 40 days later, you get your fruit and then the rest of the season the bulbs multiply under the ground. And in October it goes into dormancy till about February with wakes up again and starts the process all by itself. Englebrecht has found that the multiplication underground takes 3 years to reap the most profitable yield, so while he was literally - waiting for flowers to grow - he came up with an “out grower” business strategy – called SAFFRICON which rents out the corms to other farmers creating a new market, but also strategically finding out where else the fussy flower will grow successfully. Saffricon decided that we we're not selling corms. We're renting them out basically for three years. And then after three years, because they multiply, um, up to twenty seven times in three years, um, we buy all those corms back again from those outgrowers. Engelbrechts farm-hands joke that they’ve broken their backs with Englebrecht, not for him. AFRIKAANS – I’m I want them to grow with me in this business. And to take ownership. and you can see the pride. This soccer-field sized crop will rake in a million rand. Englebrecht’s team are also hand delivering these starter-packs to small scale farmers around the country. B: I don't want to give out hectres of this, this, and then everybody is cross with me because it didn't work. And the best thing to do is to make sure that it works with you. And then next year you can make an educated decision by yourself. SAFFRON PROVIDES A BEAUTIFUL GOLDEN COLOUR AND A PUNGEANT, AROMATIC FLAVOUR TO FOOD… THE RED GOLD THREATS ARE SOLD IN A FEW STRANDS OR IN GROUND FORM. IT ALSO HAS MANY OTHER USES – IN MEDICINE, PERFUME AND DYES… AND IT’S THE COLOUR AND SMELL THAT DETERMINE THE QUALITY. We met up with the team in Johannesburg who have found an international buyer. B: Iran is the biggest producer. They do about 300 tons of saffron a year. Mac: This is a korm? “Komm saam met my hahaha” B: We just got feedback, from a sheikh in Bahrain that wants to buy all our from that. The quality's extremely good. M: How much would saffron this much be about? B: I would say that's about five, five grams, about ten grand. M: Ten grand. So I'm holding ten grand. Yeah. Yeah. Ten thousand. Yeah. Wow. And to filll this? B: two day's work depending on how many people you have working with you and doing M: Two days just for this much? B: Yeah. Farm worker NORTH OF PRETORIA, A SMALL SCALE FARMING PROJECT HAS BEEN SET UP TO PLANT SAFFRON. MARCH IS PLANTING SEASON, AND BY THE END OF APRIL, THE FLOWERS WILL BE READY TO HARVEST. Jaco Fick is a painter – but upon hearing about the lucrative opportunity decided it was worth digging up his family’s plot and planting the picky flower. M: When did this operation start? J: Basically from breaking soil, uh, three weeks, three weeks. M: Wow. And are you excited? J: Yes, we are. We are totally excited. We are really looking forward to what this can actually become. Adlib J: Basically if we are going to do it we need to do it 100%. Farming solutions expert Corné Liebenberg shares Englebrecht’s vision, but also SAFFRICON. As co-director, he’s assisting investors in cultivating the spice - successfully. Mac: What's the excitement around saffron? Corne: Most probably, the potential income stream. We started I think about 300 of the corms and now there’s more than two million. So it's a good success story. You have to create a market and a good brand and I think that’s going to create a bigger market, because currently the market is way higher than the supply. Mac: So kids, we can stop saying Old MacDonald had a farm. They can say old Macfarlane had a farm... Englebrecht has gifted a starter pack to the local Calvinia municipality hoping they become as excited about the flower as he is. Back on the farm it seems even the weather - which has brought rain - is spurring on Englebrecht to succeed. E: Very, very nice surprise last night when 25. Mm. And, um, basically the soil was prepared for us for today. Using modern farming techniques like a planting machine, the team cut down a week long process to only a few hours. For now, it's very crucial that we don't go overboard and go too quickly we need to do our homework and make sure that it works right now. Engelbrechts ‘can do’ attitude will hopefully see that careful homework rewarded… for now though, he’s content to while away the time waiting for his saffron to grow, reading his own poetry on his stoep in the vast karoo landscape…(poetry)

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): At R200,000 rand for 1 kg, Saffron is the most expensive spice. However, SA farmers have tried and failed for years to produce a viable, sellable crop. But that was until now.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The land of Saffron In 2016 Northern Cape farm Bennie Englebrecht decided to try planting SAFFRON. Despite previous farmers trying and abandoning the challenge quite quickly in South Africa. Bennie managed to grow excellent crops (based on both smell and flavour). Saffron is the MOST expensive spice in the world at R200,000 for one kilogram. Englebrecht however took several years to make the saffron profitable because the downer about it is that it takes 150,000 crocus sativus flowers to yield ONE kilogram – and that means you need labour – each corm/flower/bulb producers 3 red threads (stigma’s - tiny thin red threat part of the flower) The production is very labour intensive, however the flowers are frost resistant and don’t need much water – but lots of heat – which is perfect for karoo like conditions. Engelbrecht created “Saffricon” and is the managing director – he has tried and tested his crop over 4 years (his farm is between Williston and calvinia in the northern cape (about 4.5 hours from cape town). Based on his quality – he had interest from Bahrain who believes there is a strong demand for this product internationally. The only other country that has been successful is Iran – and that’s because the majority of its labour force are woman who are paid $5 per day. But its not just used as a spice. Its also used for medicine, dyes and cigarettes. Englebrecht came up with an idea to assist local farmers to start their own crops – his company company is now making saffron bulbs available for around R450,000 for 150,000 of these so-called corms, which should cover a quarter hectare, as part of growing contracts.
metadata.Summary: He is doing this to solve a two fold problem: 1. To ensure that the market grows and assists developing farmers – this week he is in northern pretoria assisting up and coming potential farmers beginning their crops, ad 2. To find out where else in south Africa it will grow successfully. Within three years, peak production should deliver between 1kg and 5kg saffron a hectare. While the sterile flowers are delicate, they only need 250mm to 300m in irrigation, are frost resistant and can withstand temperatures of minus 15 degrees Celsius. Engelbrecht believes the plants are best suited to the Karoo, but Saffricon is currently testing in KwaZulu-Natal and elsewhere as well. Plans are in place that could see South Africa becoming a significant player in the farming and export of saffron. For the South African economy, this offers an invaluable source of foreign income from exports, whilst also assisting in establishing emerging, small-scale farmers - Furthermore, it offers commercial farmers an alternative source of income through diversification.
metadata.Further information: ABOUT SAFFRICON: This will be accomplished through an outgrower (contract grower) system based on three-year contracts with farmers. “We supply the farmers with our saffron corms (bulbs), which they then plant and cultivate before harvesting the saffron threads (made up of the crimson-coloured stigmas and styles) and selling the annual crop back to us. The corms multiply underground, on average, about three times per year – that means if one corm is planted in year one, you will, on average, have three corms in year two, nine in year three, 27 in year four, and so on. “The corms are sold back to Saffricon after year three, hence farmers’ take-up is guaranteed, and they have a double-income potential: from the annual saffron harvest, as well as from the multiplied corms.” Saffricon has started marketing the outgrower system to prospective saffron farmers and expect to have built sufficient corm stock by next year to start gaining momentum. “This year, there is limited corm stock available and only a few hand-picked outgrowers will be supplied with the product. But by 2022, we should be able to help many more. So, interested parties should start placing orders with Saffricon (www.saffricon.co.za) as soon as possible in order to not be disappointed.” One farmer who is trying this: Corne Liebenberg of agriculture company Laeveld Agrochem is trying to grow this in Northern Pretoria. “LAC wants to assist and uplift as far as possible, and the saffron venture offers many farmers that are currently under pressure an alternative option, whilst at the same time giving small-scale farmers an opportunity with solid prospects. “It is ideal for niche farming – a huge growth area for the South African economy and something that LAC is very passionate about. The initial capital outlay is manageable, relatively little space is required (250m² can accommodate 15 000 corms), and Saffricon will assist with training to bring new farmers up to speed,” says Liebenberg. “The outgrower (contract grower) system will uplift especially rural communities and give them a means to not only provide for their basic necessities, but also assist them to establish their own businesses with good growth possibilities. Concomitantly, the farmer does not have to wait very long for his return as is the case with many other crops. The above-ground plant growth and eventual harvesting of the flowers happen relatively quickly after the corm is planted. The farming of saffron is also ideally suited to the South African climate – which, in the last few years, has gone through a harsh drought – as it requires much less water compared to many of the large traditional crops in South Africa,” adds Liebenberg. Where South Africa’s most prevalent annual crops require roughly between 500-800mm of irrigation per season, saffron – a winter crop grown from March to October – needs between 250mm and 300mm per season. Liebenberg continues: “Saffron can be grown in almost any environment, in conditions that are traditionally not ideally suited for most kinds of agriculture – such as the Northern Cape, which actually suits the cultivation of saffron. Hence it allows for the production of profitable vegetation from unprofitable soil. Furthermore, not only is the saffron plant frost-resistant, but it is also protected from adverse weather elements like hail for a large part of the year because of its corms being underground. The latter, and the fact that the corms are not edible, will hopefully also keep it out of the hands of petty criminals looking for food.” In South Africa, saffron (sometimes referred to as “red gold”) retails for as much as R250/g (or R250 000/kg). The hefty price tag is attributed to the labour-intensive harvesting methods followed – from picking the flowers to removing the threads – which is all done by hand. According to Engelbrecht, 150 000 flowers are needed for 1kg of saffron. “And there are three threads per flower, which means 450 000 (dried) threads are needed for 1kg of saffron. The return per hectare, in year three when production peaks, can vary between 1kg to 5kg.” GROWTH; Engelbrecht foresees solid growth prospects for the international saffron market, primarily because world demand far exceeds supply. According to a report by Grand View Research, the global saffron market size was valued at US$881.7 million (about R13.4 billion) in 2019, with expected compound annual growth of 7.3%, reaching US$1.6 billion (about R22.4 billion) in 2027. Grand View Research base their findings on a growing food industry, improved standard of living, and increasing consumer disposable income.
